30: [Translation of the terumah discussion only; other discussions in this section are not translated.] Regarding terumah (priestly offerings), one does not change food into a liquid except for olives and grapes alone. Based on this, dates that are terumah should not be made into beer, nor should honey be made from them. Similarly, beer should not be made from apples, nor vinegar from late-season grapes. Late-season grapes are those that remain attached to the vine until autumn because their nature is such that they do not ripen until that time. These grapes are suitable only for vinegar, not for wine. Likewise, for all other fruits, one does not convert them from a solid state into a liquid, as their extracted liquid is considered mere moisture and not significant enough to be classified as terumah—except for olives and grapes, as explained. Nevertheless, if the liquid was already extracted, one may drink it while maintaining the purity of terumah. If someone drinks it unknowingly (without realizing it was terumah), they are exempt even from repaying the principal amount, and certainly, they are not required to add the usual fifth. This ruling has already been written in Tractate Chullin. However, one may crush a terumah fruit or cut it into small pieces with a knife without concern.
